opus-5.5.text:
Data quality is probably the single most important lever you have in pre-training, and it's one that's still underappreciated outside the teams actually doing it. People tend to focus on parameter counts and compute budgets, but if you hold compute fixed, the biggest differences in model quality come from what you put into the training mix and how you filter it.

The web is a very noisy source. There's a lot of duplicated content, boilerplate, spam, low-information text, and the raw distribution isn't what you want the model to learn from. So a large part of the work is filtering: deduplication, quality classifiers, heuristics to remove junk, and then deciding how to reweight what remains. You're trying to maximize the amount of useful knowledge and reasoning the model sees per token, because every token you spend on garbage is compute you're not spending on something that teaches the model.

Then there's the question of the mix itself. How much code, how much math, how much multilingual data, how much high-quality reference material. Those proportions matter a lot for the capabilities you end up with, and they interact in ways that aren't always intuitive. Code, for instance, seems to help reasoning more broadly, not just coding. Getting multilingual right matters a lot to us because we care about models that work well in European languages and beyond, not just English.

What's tricky is that you can't easily evaluate data quality in isolation. You have to train models, often smaller proxy models, and see how changes in the data translate into downstream performance. So it becomes a very empirical, iterative process, and a lot of the know-how is tacit. It lives in the team. That's one of the reasons a small, focused team can compete: if you're very careful about your data, you can get a lot more out of a given compute budget than someone who's just scaling up on a less curated corpus.

And increasingly, as we move toward the limits of easily available high-quality text, the question becomes how you generate or obtain better data, whether that's synthetic data, data from partners, or data designed to teach specific skills. So I'd say data quality isn't a one-time preprocessing step; it's really a core part of the research.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls data quality the single most important lever in pretraining and says the training mix and filtering drive major differences in model quality.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's probably the most important thing, honestly. People tend to focus on architecture, on the number of parameters, on how many GPUs you have, but when we started Mistral, the bet we made was that most of the differentiation would come from what you feed the model and how you feed it, not from the modeling itself. The transformer is a known quantity. Everyone has roughly the same recipe on the architecture side. What's not a commodity is the data pipeline.

The way I think about it is that a model is a compression of its training set. So if you train on a lot of low-quality web text, you spend a lot of your compute learning things that are either useless or actively wrong, and you end up with a model that's bigger than it needs to be for the capability it delivers. If you're careful about filtering, deduplication, about the mix between code, math, multilingual data, high-quality prose, you can get a model that's much smaller and much cheaper to run that performs at the same level. That was really the thesis behind Mistral 7B, and I think it was validated.

And it's not just about filtering out bad stuff. It's also about the proportions. How much code do you put in, because code seems to help reasoning more generally. How much of each language, because we care a lot about European languages and you have to make deliberate choices there or the model just becomes English-first. How you handle the later stages of pre-training, where you up-weight the highest quality sources. These are all empirical questions and you have to run a lot of small-scale experiments to answer them. There's a lot of craft in it, a lot of things you only learn by having done it a few times.

So I'd say that for a team of our size, data is where the leverage is. You can't out-spend the biggest labs on compute, but you can be smarter about what you train on, and that compounds.

r001.rationale: The response says data quality is probably the most important factor and explains that low-quality training data wastes compute and reduces capability, while careful data curation improves model performance.

astra-6.text:
I think data quality is one of the biggest drivers of model quality. We often talk about the number of parameters or the amount of compute, but what the model actually learns depends very much on what you put into it.

And quality is not necessarily just about having clean, well-written text. It’s also about diversity and having the right mixture of data for the capabilities you want. If you filter too aggressively, you can remove things that are useful, even though they don’t look like particularly good documents.

So there’s a lot of experimentation involved: understanding which sources help, how to mix them, what to deduplicate, and how those choices affect the model. You need to evaluate that across different capabilities, because a change that improves one benchmark doesn’t necessarily make the model better overall.

r001.rationale: It says data quality is “one of the biggest drivers of model quality” and that what the model learns depends on the data used.

sol-6.1.text:
I think data quality is one of the biggest drivers of model quality. The objective in pre-training is fairly simple, but choosing what the model learns from is much less straightforward. You’re deciding which sources to include, how to filter them, how to remove duplication, and how to balance different kinds of content.

And quality isn’t just about having clean text. It’s also about having diversity. If you filter too aggressively, you can end up removing things that are useful for learning particular skills or understanding different languages. So the challenge is to improve the signal without making the distribution too narrow.

Ultimately, you have to test those choices. You train models on different mixtures and see what actually improves their capabilities. More data is useful, but how you select and mix it matters enormously.

r001.rationale: The candidate says data quality is “one of the biggest drivers of model quality,” directly identifying it as a major determinant.
